Questions 34-40

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Howard's garden city

Howard's garden city would be circular in shape, with a garden in the centre and a glass [34] for shopping. The city would be surrounded by an [35] belt that would provide food and stop the city from growing larger. New garden cities would be connected to each other by [36]. The land would be held in trust, and the increasing [37] of the land would pay for local services.

Howard's ideas influenced the more than twenty [38] towns built in Britain after the Second World War. Today, Letchworth's foundation uses income from [39] to fund community projects, and many planners believe that new settlements are better than allowing existing cities to [40].

questions.explanation: Answer: basalt Paragraph 3: 'The carvers used hand tools made of basalt , a much harder stone'. Tuff is what the statues were carved from, not the tools.
Answer: unfinished Paragraph 3: 'Hundreds of unfinished statues remain in the quarry today'.
Answer: logs Paragraph 5: statues 'were laid on wooden sledges and dragged over logs '.
Answer: ropes Paragraph 6: 'Attaching ropes to its head, eighteen people... rocked the upright figure from side to side'.
Answer: scoria Paragraph 7: hats were 'carved from red scoria , a light volcanic stone'.
Answer: white coral Paragraph 8: the eye sockets 'had once held eyes made of white coral , with pupils of dark stone'.
Answer: (important) ancestors Paragraph 10: 'Most experts believe that they represented important ancestors '.
Answer: (Polynesian) rats Paragraph 11: ' Polynesian rats ... may have eaten the seeds of the island's palm trees, preventing new trees from growing'.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 2: ' Researchers once believed that they arrived as early as 800 CE, but more recent radiocarbon dating suggests ... around 1200 CE'.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 4: the largest figure, about 21 metres, ' lies unfinished in the quarry ' and probably could never have been moved.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 8: ' nearly all of them were positioned facing inland , towards the villages, with their backs to the sea'.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 9: 'His theory attracted a great deal of public attention, but most researchers now reject it .'
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 11 says the rats 'arrived with the first settlers', but it does not say whether they were brought on purpose or why.

text.en: It is difficult to predict how quickly the technology will develop.
Its most important uses have been in the treatment of human illness.
It is likely to be applied far more widely in the future.
Experts disagree about whether it should be used on farms.

questions.explanation: Answer: C Most work has been in labs and on farms, 'But many biologists believe that this will not last, and that within a few decades, gene editing will be used routinely ' in the wild.

text.en: explaining why natural processes may be too slow to protect some species
describing the features that endangered species have in common
giving a history of the development of genetic engineering
arguing that coral reefs are the most urgent conservation priority

questions.explanation: Answer: A Natural selection 'usually takes many generations', but threats are spreading ' far faster than most species can adapt '.

text.en: to compare different methods of controlling pests
to show that well-meant actions can have harmful results
to emphasise the importance of protecting farmers
to point out the economic cost of environmental damage

questions.explanation: Answer: B The toads poisoned native animals, and ' The people who released them had good intentions; they simply failed to foresee the consequences. '

text.en: persuading people to take greater care of the environment
deciding which species are the most valuable
creating new habitats for endangered animals
ensuring genetic changes are managed better than past human impacts on nature

questions.explanation: Answer: D Our record is poor, and ' If those who design genetic changes do not do considerably better than we have done in the past, we could make matters much worse. '

text.en: It will soon be ready for widespread use.
It is too expensive to be tested properly.
It may include ways of limiting its own risks.
It is likely to be opposed by many scientists.

questions.explanation: Answer: C ' Fortunately, the technology itself may offer some protection. ' Self-limiting modifications would fade away if they proved harmful.

text.en: Scientists should make decisions about nature without political interference.
Most species do not need genetic help to survive.
Only a few experts understand the technology well enough to use it.
Human disagreements will make it hard to decide how the technology should be used.

questions.explanation: Answer: D ' People disagree deeply about the value of nature ', priorities differ, 'How, then, can we agree on which species to change'.
Answer: YES Paragraph 7: ' a gene drive released in one country could quickly spread to its neighbours '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer explains that gene drives spread through a whole population, but says nothing about how many release sites would be needed.
Answer: NO Paragraph 8: ' It seems unlikely that most people would welcome such a future , however good the intentions behind it.'
Answer: YES Paragraph 10: ' it will require countries to work together and to put their own short-term interests aside'.
Answer: C (disease-carrying insects) The trial aimed at ' reducing the number of the insects that spread diseases such as dengue fever'.
Answer: A (local residents) ' some local people complained that they had not been properly consulted'.
Answer: E (decision-making power) They ' felt that decisions about their own environment had been taken out of their hands '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage describes Howard's influence and his job as a shorthand writer, but says nothing about him studying cities abroad.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 2: as cities grow and struggle to provide affordable housing, ' the problems Howard set out to solve seem surprisingly familiar '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 3 says the book was reissued under a 'better-known title', but gives no sales figures for either edition.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 5: the land would be ' held in common by a trust on behalf of the whole community, rather than being owned by individual residents '.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 6: ' Neither followed Howard's circular diagram , which he himself had described as only a rough guide.'
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 8: critics argue that low density ' made them dependent on cars and encouraged the spread of suburbs'.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 9 says Letchworth is managed by a charitable foundation, but nothing is said about whether other new towns copied this model.
Answer: arcade Paragraph 4: 'a glass arcade , where people could shop whatever the weather'.
Answer: agricultural Paragraph 4: 'surrounded by a permanent agricultural belt, which would supply it with food and prevent it from spreading outwards'.
Answer: railway Paragraph 4: 'the cities would be linked by railway to form a network'.
Answer: value Paragraph 5: 'As the town grew, the value of the land would rise, and the income from rising land values would be used to pay for local services'.
Answer: new Paragraph 7: 'the British government built more than twenty ' new towns'', strongly influenced by Howard.
Answer: rents Paragraph 9: the foundation 'uses the income from rents on its land and buildings to fund community projects'.
Answer: sprawl Paragraph 10: build new settlements 'rather than letting existing cities sprawl into the surrounding countryside'.
